nameStory: The oblong-winged katydid gets its name from the distinctive elongated, oval shape of its wings, which are noticeably longer and more stretched out than those of its round-winged cousins. While most katydids have fairly circular or broad wings, this species sports wings that are clearly oblong - like little green ovals attached to its body.
description: The oblong-winged katydid is a medium-sized green insect that looks like a leaf with legs and long antennae. These katydids are part of the round-headed katydid group, distinguished by their relatively broad heads and prominent eyes. They're excellent camouflage artists, blending seamlessly into the foliage where they spend their time munching on leaves and calling to potential mates. Like other katydids, they're most active at night when their chirping songs fill the summer air.

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Wings are distinctly oblong or oval-shaped, noticeably longer than they are wide, extending well past the abdomen when folded. The wing edges feel papery and thin to the touch.

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Head appears broad and rounded when viewed from the front, giving it a somewhat flattened appearance compared to other katydids.

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Bright green coloration that matches fresh leaves, sometimes with subtle yellowish tinge. The green is uniform and vibrant, not mottled or spotted.

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Very long, thread-like antennae that are often longer than the entire body, constantly moving and twitching as they feel their surroundings.

idTips.label: Sound
idTips.description: Males produce a soft, rhythmic chirping at night that sounds like 'tick-tick-tick' rather than the harsh 'katy-did' call of true katydids.

habitat: Look for oblong-winged katydids in deciduous forests, woodland edges, and shrubland throughout New England's lower elevations. They prefer areas with dense foliage, especially where oak, maple, and other broad-leaved trees provide plenty of cover and food. You'll often find them in the understory vegetation and shrub layer rather than high in the tree canopy.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet present in spring. Look for tiny nymphs starting to appear in late spring, resembling miniature wingless versions of adults.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for spotting adults from July through August. Listen for their soft nighttime calls and look for them on leaves during the day when they're resting.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with calling continuing into September. This is often the best time to spot them as vegetation begins to thin.
seasonality.winter: No adults present. Eggs overwinter in plant tissue or soil, completely dormant until spring warmth triggers development.

funFact: Oblong-winged katydids are accomplished leaf mimics that even sway gently when there's no breeze, copying the natural movement of leaves to avoid detection by sharp-eyed birds and other predators.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the rattler round-winged katydid, but remember 'oblong vs. round' - if the wings look stretched out like ovals rather than circular, you've found the oblong-winged species. The wing shape difference is obvious once you know what to look for.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'katydids,' oblong-winged katydids don't actually make the classic 'katy-did' sound - that's reserved for true katydids in a different group. The katydid family name comes from the few species that do make that distinctive call, but it's been applied to the whole diverse family of bush crickets.
compareHints: Among its round-headed katydid relatives in New England, the oblong-winged katydid is distinguished by those characteristic elongated wings, while the rattler round-winged katydid has notably circular wings. The carinate katydid, when present, has a distinctive ridge or 'keel' running down its back that the oblong-winged species lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its Oblong-winged cousin, the Rattler Round-winged Katydid has distinctly rounded rather than elongated wing tips and typically produces a more continuous rattling call.
